top.line: Checking every output is a bottleneck and weak net
top.para: Asked whether the human in the loop is a safety net or bottleneck, I answer that checking every output is both and mostly neither: people approve 93% of permission prompts. Put people where outputs cannot be undone and the blast radius is large, use tireless controls elsewhere, and let the record move the line.

in-short.line: The question is where a human belongs, not whether
in-short.para: Checking everything does not scale and rarely catches anything. People belong at sending in my name, typing secrets, spending money and unrecoverable deletion; elsewhere validators, a second reader, enforced policy rows and a record do better. Reviews should fix the source, trust grows from drafts nobody changed, and this newsroom ships unapproved while my email waits.

question.line: A roundtable asked: safety net or bottleneck?
question.para: Someone shaping a roundtable in London asked whether the human in the loop is a safety net or a bottleneck. Many companies have impressive agent pilots, yet few trust an agent to decide without someone checking every output. They also asked how far I had got with AI in production.

both.line: Checking everything costs a bottleneck, protects like a stamp
both.para: An agent waiting on a person runs at the person's speed. Anthropic found Claude Code users approve 93% of permission prompts, named approval fatigue, and cut prompts by 84% with sandboxing. A person asked for a yes with little context or authority is where liability lands, not a safety net.

where.line: Put people where outputs are irreversible and costly
where.para: Two questions place every output: can it be undone, and what would it cost if wrong? Where it cannot be undone and the blast radius is large, a person should make a real decision, as with sending email in my name, typing secrets, spending money and deleting without backup. Elsewhere a person is the wrong control.

controls.line: Tireless controls replace human checks on reversible outputs
controls.para: Articles here are reversible, so validators, browser tests and leak scans stand in the way, and I read after publication. A second reader the agent cannot skip checks every email draft, like banks' maker-checker. Redesigning one customer service agent cut its hope-only policy from 97% to 23% and its reach from 38,000 records to one.

source.line: Good reviews fix the source, not just the output
source.para: A review should improve whatever produced the draft, the rule, prompt or data, rather than the draft itself. My corrections to wording become rules in the session's behaviour policy, and How the voice works found almost all corrections now concern content and direction. A source-fixing reviewer is needed less every week.

record.line: A record of unchanged drafts earns agents more room
record.para: Trust in my email agents is a record of drafts sent unchanged, each hash beside the sent email. When that record is long enough, a message type can leave the human step by a written, owned, dated policy decision; so far only a security agent's hold email has. Reading footprints afterwards catches unseen near misses.

production.line: Fourteen unapproved releases in a day, zero sent emails
production.para: On 13 October 2026 the newsroom shipped fourteen releases, v0.12.5 to v0.12.18, every commit by an agent and none approved beforehand, with five articles published and read afterwards. Meanwhile twelve correspondence agents draft every email and send none. It is one rule applied to two blast radii: articles can be corrected, emails cannot.

roundtable.line: Questions to find where your people really belong
roundtable.para: Which outputs can be undone, and are people only on the others? What is the approver shown, could they refuse, and if over ninety per cent of approvals are yes, what is the check for? Which checks could be validators or platform boundaries, and what record would let a human check go next quarter?

limits.line: One vendor's figure and one small production setup
limits.para: The 93% concerns permission prompts in one coding agent. My production is one person, one newsroom and one agent team, so the pattern rather than the scale is defended. Medicine, law and moving others' money keep their own rules, nobody approving releases does not mean nobody is responsible, and the roundtable question is paraphrased.

sources.line: Sources: a private question, Anthropic posts, git log
sources.para: The article answers a private message of 13 October 2026 from an unnamed roundtable organiser and was assembled from my published positions, with no voice memo. Anthropic's figures come from How we built Claude Code auto mode and Beyond permission prompts, and production counts from the newsroom's git log.
